title: How to Start a Hospice Program in California: Complete Licensing Guide

html:
Introduction

California’s hospice industry serves tens of thousands of individuals and families navigating end-of-life care annually. As the nation’s most populous state with a significant aging population, California offers meaningful opportunities for entrepreneurs committed to providing compassionate hospice care. The demand for quality end-of-life services continues to grow.

The California Department of Public Health (CDPH) licenses and regulates hospice programs through comprehensive standards designed to ensure quality care during life’s most vulnerable moments. Understanding these requirements—from licensure through ongoing compliance—is essential for success in this specialized healthcare sector.

This comprehensive guide covers everything you need to know about starting a licensed hospice program in California, from regulatory requirements to operational excellence in palliative and end-of-life care.

Table of Contents

  • Understand California’s Regulations
  • Choose the Type and Size of Program
  • Business Structure and Licensing
  • Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan
  • Secure a Suitable Facility and Location
  • Hire and Train Qualified Staff
  • Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans
  • Marketing and Community Outreach
  • Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Inspections
  • Frequently Asked Questions

1. Understand California’s Regulations

California maintains rigorous hospice regulations that align with and sometimes exceed federal requirements. Understanding this regulatory landscape is essential.

Regulatory Authority

The California Department of Public Health (CDPH), Licensing and Certification Division, oversees hospice licensure. Key regulatory requirements include:

  • State licensure under California Health and Safety Code
  • Medicare certification for hospices seeking Medicare reimbursement
  • Medi-Cal certification for California Medicaid participation
  • Compliance with Title 22 of California Code of Regulations
  • Federal Conditions of Participation for Medicare-certified hospices

Hospice Service Components

California hospice programs must provide or arrange for:

  • Nursing services available 24 hours daily
  • Physician services including hospice medical director
  • Medical social services for psychosocial support
  • Counseling services including bereavement
  • Hospice aide and homemaker services
  • Physical, occupational, and speech therapy as needed
  • Dietary counseling
  • Short-term inpatient care for symptom management or respite
  • Medical supplies and equipment
  • Medications for pain and symptom management

The Medicare Hospice Benefit

Most hospice care is covered under the Medicare Hospice Benefit, which requires:

  • Terminal prognosis of six months or less if disease runs normal course
  • Patient election of hospice care
  • Palliative care focus rather than curative treatment
  • Interdisciplinary team providing comprehensive care
  • Bereavement services for family members

2. Choose the Type and Size of Program

Strategic planning about your hospice’s scope and service delivery model is essential.

Service Delivery Models

Routine Home Care is the primary level of care, with most patients receiving services in their homes. This requires mobile clinical teams and 24/7 nursing availability.

Continuous Home Care provides intensive nursing care during periods of crisis. Requires minimum of 8 hours nursing/aide services in 24-hour period with nursing comprising more than half.

Inpatient Care for symptom management or procedures requires contracted or owned inpatient facility beds.

Respite Care provides short-term inpatient stays (up to 5 days) to relieve family caregivers.

Facility Considerations

Decide whether to:

Contract for inpatient services with hospitals, skilled nursing facilities, or freestanding inpatient units. Most startup hospices use this model initially.

Develop owned inpatient capacity through hospice house or dedicated unit. Requires significant capital but provides control over environment and care.

Partner with residential care facilities for routine care in assisted living or other residential settings.

Geographic Scope

Consider your service area carefully:

  • Single county focus for intensive market penetration
  • Multi-county region for volume but increased travel
  • Urban focus for higher census potential
  • Rural areas for underserved markets (may qualify for rural add-on payments)

Capacity Planning

Plan realistic growth:

  • Startup phase: Average daily census (ADC) of 15-30 patients
  • Growth phase: ADC of 50-100 patients
  • Established hospice: ADC of 150+ patients

Medicare requires demonstrating capacity for core services, so plan staffing accordingly.

3. Business Structure and Licensing

Entity Formation

Choose appropriate business structure:

Nonprofit Corporation (501(c)(3)) offers tax advantages and community benefit positioning. Many hospices operate as nonprofits given the mission-driven nature of end-of-life care.

For-Profit Corporation or LLC is increasingly common in hospice industry. May access different capital sources but faces different community perceptions.

Register with California Secretary of State and obtain EIN from IRS.

State Licensure Process

The CDPH hospice licensing process involves:

  • Submit license application with comprehensive documentation
  • Pay licensing fees (approximately $4,000-6,000)
  • Demonstrate compliance with facility and operational requirements
  • Pass background checks for owners and key personnel
  • Complete initial survey by CDPH surveyors
  • Address any deficiencies identified
  • Receive license upon successful completion

Medicare Certification

Medicare certification is essential for sustainable operations:

  • State licensure as prerequisite
  • CMS-855A enrollment application
  • Accreditation survey OR state certification survey
  • Demonstration of compliance with Conditions of Participation
  • Medicare provider number assignment

Accreditation Options

Most hospices pursue accreditation through:

  • Community Health Accreditation Partner (CHAP)
  • Accreditation Commission for Health Care (ACHC)
  • The Joint Commission

Accreditation provides deemed status for Medicare and may expedite certification.

Insurance Requirements

Obtain comprehensive coverage:

  • Professional liability: $1-3 million per occurrence
  • General liability: $1 million minimum
  • Workers’ compensation: Required
  • Directors and officers insurance: Recommended for governance protection
  • Vehicle insurance: For clinical staff using personal or agency vehicles

4. Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan

A thorough business plan guides operations and secures financing.

Market Analysis

Research your market thoroughly:

  • Demographics: Age 65+ population, terminal illness prevalence
  • Referral sources: Hospitals, oncologists, SNFs, home health agencies
  • Competition: Existing hospices, market share, service quality
  • Underserved areas: Geographic or diagnostic gaps in current services
  • Payer landscape: Medicare, Medi-Cal managed care penetration

Financial Projections

Develop realistic projections:

Startup Costs (estimated $200,000-$500,000):

  • Licensure and certification fees
  • Accreditation costs
  • Office/facility setup
  • Clinical software and EMR
  • Insurance premiums
  • Marketing and community education
  • Working capital (6-12 months)

Operating Expenses:

  • Clinical staff salaries and benefits
  • Administrative personnel
  • Contracted services (physicians, pharmacy, DME)
  • Medications and supplies
  • Facility costs
  • Bereavement program
  • Volunteer program

Revenue Projections:

  • Medicare per diem rates by level of care
  • Routine home care: ~$210/day (2024 rates)
  • Continuous home care: ~$1,100/day
  • Inpatient respite: ~$500/day
  • General inpatient: ~$820/day
  • Cap amount considerations

Reimbursement Understanding

Master hospice reimbursement:

  • Per diem payment covers all hospice services
  • Cap amount limits total annual Medicare payments per beneficiary
  • Sequestration reduces payments by 2%
  • Wage index adjustments affect rates by geographic area
  • Live discharge rates affect quality metrics

5. Secure a Suitable Facility and Location

Office Requirements

Hospice programs require appropriate administrative space:

  • Private areas for staff meetings and family conferences
  • Secure storage for medications (if maintaining stock)
  • Medical records secure storage and access
  • Staff work areas for interdisciplinary team
  • On-call space for 24/7 staff availability

Location Considerations

Select location based on:

  • Central access to primary service area
  • Parking for clinical staff and visitors
  • Professional appearance for referral sources
  • Space for bereavement support groups
  • Accessibility for volunteers and community

Inpatient Relationships

Establish agreements for inpatient services:

Hospital contracts for general inpatient care during crisis.

Skilled nursing facility agreements for inpatient and respite care.

Hospice house partnerships or development for dedicated inpatient environment.

Technology Requirements

Invest in essential systems:

  • Electronic Medical Records meeting Medicare requirements
  • Point-of-care documentation for field staff
  • Scheduling and visit tracking
  • Medication management systems
  • Bereavement tracking and documentation
  • On-call and after-hours communication systems

6. Hire and Train Qualified Staff

Medical Director

Every hospice must have a Medical Director who is:

  • Licensed physician in California
  • Responsible for medical component of patient care
  • Available for consultation and oversight
  • Experienced in palliative medicine (board certification preferred)

Interdisciplinary Team

Build your core clinical team:

Registered Nurses provide skilled nursing assessment, symptom management, and care coordination. Must be California licensed with hospice/palliative experience preferred.

Licensed Vocational Nurses provide nursing care under RN supervision per California scope of practice.

Medical Social Workers provide psychosocial assessment, counseling, and resource coordination. Master’s degree required.

Chaplains/Spiritual Counselors provide spiritual support to patients and families. Clinical Pastoral Education (CPE) preferred.

Hospice Aides provide personal care under nursing supervision. Must meet training requirements.

Bereavement Counselors provide grief support to families. Various credentials accepted.

Volunteer Program

Medicare requires hospices to maintain a volunteer program:

  • 5% of patient care hours must be provided by volunteers
  • Training program for all volunteers
  • Supervision by volunteer coordinator
  • Documentation of volunteer activities
  • Various roles: Patient/family support, administrative, bereavement

Training Requirements

Comprehensive training includes:

  • Hospice philosophy and interdisciplinary approach
  • Pain and symptom management
  • Communication skills for difficult conversations
  • Cultural competency in end-of-life care
  • Grief and bereavement support
  • Documentation requirements
  • Emergency procedures
  • HIPAA and patient rights

7. Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans

Essential Policies

Develop comprehensive policies for:

Clinical Operations:

  • Patient eligibility and admission criteria
  • Certification and recertification
  • Plan of care development and updates
  • Symptom management protocols
  • Medication management
  • After-hours and on-call procedures
  • Emergency situations and pronouncement
  • Discharge and revocation

Patient and Family Rights:

  • Informed consent and election
  • Advance directives
  • Privacy and confidentiality
  • Complaint and grievance procedures
  • Transfer and revocation rights

Quality Management:

  • Quality Assessment and Performance Improvement (QAPI)
  • Outcome measurement
  • Incident reporting and investigation
  • Infection control
  • Utilization review

Bereavement Program:

  • Assessment of bereavement risk
  • Service availability and duration
  • Documentation requirements
  • Referral for complicated grief

Care Planning Requirements

Hospice care planning requires:

  • Comprehensive assessment at admission
  • Interdisciplinary care plan addressing all domains
  • Patient and family participation in planning
  • Regular IDT meetings for care coordination
  • Care plan updates at least every 15 days
  • Certification periods (two 90-day, then 60-day)

Documentation Standards

Maintain thorough documentation:

  • Election statements and consents
  • Certification and recertification
  • Comprehensive assessments
  • Care plans and updates
  • Visit notes by all disciplines
  • Medication profiles
  • IDT meeting minutes
  • Bereavement records

8. Marketing and Community Outreach

Referral Development

Build relationships with key referral sources:

Healthcare Providers:

  • Oncologists and hematologists
  • Pulmonologists and cardiologists
  • Neurologists and geriatricians
  • Hospitalists and intensivists
  • Hospital discharge planners
  • Skilled nursing facility staff

Community Resources:

  • Home health agencies
  • Area Agencies on Aging
  • Disease-specific organizations
  • Faith communities
  • Senior services

Community Education

Raise awareness about hospice:

  • Educational presentations for community groups
  • Healthcare professional education on appropriate referrals
  • End-of-life planning seminars
  • Grief support groups open to community
  • Memorial services and remembrance events

Marketing Strategies

Relationship-Based Approach:

  • Regular visits to referral sources
  • Educational in-services
  • Case conferences and consultations
  • Appreciation events

Digital Presence:

  • Professional website with resources
  • Google Business Profile
  • Social media engagement
  • Online reputation management

Community Visibility:

  • Healthcare association membership
  • Community event sponsorship
  • Media relations and storytelling
  • Published articles and resources

Quality Differentiation

Stand out through demonstrated quality:

  • Hospice Compare quality measures
  • Consumer satisfaction scores (CAHPS)
  • Family testimonials (with appropriate consent)
  • Specialized programs (dementia, pediatric, veterans)
  • Staff credentials and specializations

9. Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Inspections

Survey Preparedness

Prepare for multiple survey types:

State Licensure Surveys verify California regulatory compliance.

Medicare Certification Surveys verify Conditions of Participation compliance.

Accreditation Surveys conducted by chosen accrediting body.

Complaint Investigations may occur at any time.

Continuous Compliance

Maintain ongoing compliance through:

  • Daily documentation review
  • Weekly IDT meeting audits
  • Monthly quality indicator tracking
  • Quarterly QAPI reporting
  • Annual policy reviews
  • Regular mock surveys

Quality Improvement

Implement robust QAPI program:

  • Data collection on quality measures
  • Trend analysis and benchmarking
  • Performance improvement projects
  • Staff involvement in quality
  • Governing body oversight

Common Deficiencies

Prepare to avoid common issues:

  • Incomplete or untimely documentation
  • Missed certification periods
  • Inadequate care plan updates
  • Insufficient IDT involvement
  • Bereavement program deficiencies
  • Volunteer program issues
  • QAPI documentation gaps

10. Frequently Asked Questions

How long does it take to open a hospice in California?

The process typically takes 9-18 months from planning to patient admission. State licensure takes 6-12 months, and Medicare certification adds additional time. Using an accrediting organization may expedite certification.

How is hospice different from palliative care?

Hospice is a specific Medicare benefit for patients with terminal prognosis who elect comfort-focused care. Palliative care is a broader specialty providing symptom management at any disease stage alongside curative treatment. Many hospices also offer palliative care programs.

Can a for-profit company own a hospice in California?

Yes, for-profit hospices operate in California and represent a growing segment of the industry. Both nonprofit and for-profit hospices must meet the same licensure and certification requirements.

How much does it cost to start a hospice in California?

Startup costs typically range from $200,000 to $500,000, including licensure, accreditation, office setup, staffing, and working capital. Costs vary based on geographic area and service model choices.

What are the biggest challenges for new hospices?

Common challenges include building referral relationships, managing length of stay and cap, staffing (especially nursing), and achieving average daily census for financial sustainability. Strong community relationships and quality outcomes drive long-term success.

Conclusion

Starting a hospice program in California requires deep commitment to compassionate end-of-life care alongside rigorous compliance with regulatory requirements. The state’s large population and growing acceptance of hospice services create meaningful opportunity for dedicated providers.

Success depends on building strong clinical programs, comprehensive interdisciplinary teams, and genuine community relationships. Quality care for patients and families drives referrals and sustainable growth.
